title: Remember, and find peace
hook: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remember, remember, and find peace (Sukhmani 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani's opening salok, and your line: I bow. Did you lower your head before something serious? Today, the first stanza, and the word the whole bani rests on. Day four hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `I BOW — FOUR BOWS TO THE GURU.`

segments.voice: How do you remember a phone number someone just told you? You say it again. And again. Under your breath, all the way to the pen. How do you remember a person who has died? You say their name, tell their stories, keep their photo where you'll see it. Remembering, it turns out, is mostly repetition. Not a single grand act, but something done again and again until it becomes part of you. That is exactly how the first stanza of Sukhmani begins: with one word, said three times in a row.
screen: `A PHONE NUMBER, SAID AGAIN.` → `A NAME, A STORY, A PHOTO.` → `REMEMBERING IS REPETITION.`

segments.voice: The first stanza opens: simro simar simar sukh paavo. I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. Then, in paraphrase: and the troubles and anguish of the body are erased. The word under all of it is simran. It comes from the Sanskrit smarana, remembering, from a root meaning to remember or call to mind. In Sikh life, simran means remembering God, and in practice it often means repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, again and again. Listen to how the line performs what it describes. Simro, simar, simar: the word itself is repeated, three beats before the reward arrives. Sukh paavo: I find peace. Sukh, the same sukh as in Sukhmani. So the jewel of peace you met two days ago is found, right here at the start, by remembering. The stanza goes on to say, in paraphrase, that the Vedas, the Puranas and the Simritis, the great scriptures of Guru Arjan's world, were made from the one word of the Name. And that the person in whose heart even a tiny particle of it lives has a glory no one can count. Then it closes, as the stanzas will, with Nanak's voice: those who long only for the sight of You, save me with them. Here's what makes simran different from just thinking about God. Thinking is something you do once and finish. Simran is a practice. It's a phone number said over and over until your mouth knows it before your mind does. The stanza promises that peace is found in that repeating.
screen: `SIMRO SIMAR SIMAR: REMEMBER, AGAIN.` · `SIMRAN, FROM SMARANA.` · `THE ONE WORD THE SCRIPTURES CAME FROM.` · `A PRACTICE, NOT A THOUGHT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, FIND PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat the Name ten times. If you pray, say Waheguru, slowly, ten times, aloud or in your head, letting each one ride on an out-breath. If that isn't your practice, choose a word that steadies you, peace, or thank you, or a name you love, and repeat it the same way. Count on your fingers if it helps. Don't hurry toward ten. When you reach it, sit in the quiet afterward and notice what's different, if anything. The bell holds the time.
Simran. Remembering God, often by repeating the Name; Sukhmani's first stanza says that remembering, again and again, brings peace.

Your line: remember, find peace. Today, pick one repeated moment, every time you unlock your phone, every time you wash your hands, and let it carry one quiet Waheguru, or your own steady word. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, alone or together in the sangat; some use a mala of beads to count, and many keep the Name going through the day's ordinary tasks.

fork.setup: you want peace, the jewel the bani is named for. what does the first stanza of Sukhmani say to do?
options: think hard about God, once, deeply.
fork.reveal: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remembering, and remembering again, you find peace.

original.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembrance; the practice Sukhmani opens with.

trapdoor: what you thought: simran means meditation in general.
what it means: remembering God, often by repeating the Name again and again, which Sukhmani says brings peace.
what a scholar hears: simran derives from Sanskrit smarana (root smr, to remember); the stanza's triple simro simar simar enacts the repetition it describes.

sources.ref: Gauri Sukhmani M5, ashtpadi 1, pauri 1, Ang 262

notes: First pauri paraphrased: 'remembering, remembering, I find peace; the troubles and anguish of the body are erased'; 'the Vedas, Puranas and Simritis were made from the one word of the Name'; 'the one in whose heart even a particle of it lives has a glory no one can count'; 'those who long only for the sight of You, save me with them'. Confirm.
Etymology simran < Sanskrit smarana (root smr): standard; confirm.
Transliteration follows the outline ('simro simar simar sukh paavo'); the usual form is 'simrau simar simar sukh paavau'. Confirm preferred spelling.
